conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. You’re off oxygen now, breathing room air at 98%. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow to extended care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Back to rehab? Will they help with swallowing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’re scheduling outpatient speech and swallow follow-up. You’ll also need a repeat endoscopy to check an ulcer found on a prior EGD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot about that. I never went for the follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll arrange it. Also, keep taking your regular meds — thyroid, statin, PPI, and the new antibiotic for seven days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the salt pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue those twice a day. We’ll monitor your sodium at rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We removed your Foley this morning. You voided 300 mL — that’s a good start. We’ll keep trying daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I can go on my own now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep encouraging it. Urology will follow up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’re being discharged today to extended care. You’ve recovered well from septic shock.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. No shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lungs still have some coarse sounds, but the infection is clearing. Keep taking amoxicillin-clavulanate twice a day for the full seven days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thick liquids, soft foods, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And someone should watch you eat. Avoid sedatives — they can make things worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. No sleeping pills unless needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep your trazodone for sleep — it’s safer than benzos. And keep all your other meds the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My brother will help me keep track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ve updated him. You’ll have follow-up with speech therapy, urology, and GI. Call if you have fever, trouble breathing, or can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up the good work. Rehab will help you stay strong and safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — your CT showed gallstones, but they’re not causing problems now. We’ll monitor, but no action needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, as long as it doesn’t hurt.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of your doctors here. You were brought in last night because you were having trouble breathing and had a fever. Can you tell me how you’re feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still short of breath. It hurts to breathe deep. And I’ve been coughing up something thick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. Your oxygen level was low, and your lungs had some infection on the right side. We started antibiotics and fluids. You were also a bit low in blood pressure, so we gave you medicine to support that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this before… from aspirating. I know I shouldn’t eat certain things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. Given your history, we’re very concerned this is another aspiration pneumonia. We’re treating it with strong antibiotics—vancomycin and Zosyn—for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another feeding tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll talk about that later. Right now, your brother is your health care proxy, and we’ll discuss your wishes together. But for now, we’re focused on treating the infection and getting your breathing better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve placed a central line in your leg to give antibiotics more safely. It helps us avoid multiple IV sticks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why my leg feels tight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s normal. We’ll keep an eye on it. You’re also getting oxygen and breathing treatments every few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your white blood cell count is high, which means your body is fighting infection. But your heart and kidneys look okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my sodium? It’s always low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s 125, which is low. We think it’s due to your body holding onto too much water—called SIADH. We’re limiting your fluids to 1200 cc per day to help correct it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s tough. I get thirsty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. We’ll give you ice chips and mouth swabs to help. Your sodium should improve as you get better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a swallow study today with the speech team. It showed you’re aspirating with all liquids—even thick ones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can’t drink anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not safely, no. We discussed this with your brother. You both understand the risks, and you’ve decided against a feeding tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want a tube. I’d rather eat, even if it’s risky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s your right. We’ve documented that in your chart. You’re DNR/DNI, meaning no resuscitation or intubation if your breathing fails. But you do want to be hospitalized if you get pneumonia again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I want treatment, just not machines to keep me alive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We respect that. Palliative care will help support your choices.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We moved your IV line from your leg to your arm today. It’s called a PICC line, and it’s safer for longer antibiotic use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why did they take the other one out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because leg lines can increase infection risk and aren’t ideal for long-term use. The PICC line in your arm is better for your treatment course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray shows the PICC tip is in your brachiocephalic vein. That’s where it should be.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I felt anxious when they said it wasn’t clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing has improved. You’re now on 2 liters of oxygen and saturating well. But your chest X-ray shows the infection has shifted to the left lung.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. It’s changing, which can happen. We’re still treating with the same antibiotics because your white count went up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought it was going down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It did, but then rose again. You’re not febrile, and your exam is stable, so we think it’s due to ongoing aspiration, not a new infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you a diuretic for fluid in your lungs. Your BNP was elevated, so there’s some heart-related fluid buildup too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not just the pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. It’s a mix: pneumonia from aspiration, COPD flare, and mild heart failure. We’re treating all three.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sodium improved to 128, but we’re keeping the fluid restriction. Your weight has been fluctuating, so we’re watching that closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been peeing more since the Lasix.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. It means the diuretic is working. We removed the Foley catheter, and you’ve been able to void on your own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing much better. You’re off pressors, on minimal oxygen, and your labs are stabilizing. We’ll keep the antibiotics for a full 8-day course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go to extended care, not home. You’ll need help with swallowing and monitoring for breathing issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll be safe there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. They’ll follow your DNR status, watch your sodium, and give your IV antibiotics until the course is done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your vancomycin level was high—21.2—so we reduced the dose to avoid kidney issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only if it stays high. We’ll check it again soon and adjust as needed. Your kidneys are fine now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest X-ray shows the lung opacities are more even, but no consolidation. There’s concern for underlying interstitial lung disease, so we’ll refer you to pulmonary clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: More tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a follow-up. It’s not urgent, but good to understand your lung health long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re stable. Still on 2L oxygen, saturating at 100%. Your breathing treatments are now scheduled regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try a little water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know you’re thirsty, but the swallow study showed you aspirate with all liquids. We can’t allow oral intake. It could lead to another pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. It’s just hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep giving you mouth care. And your brother will be here later to talk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged to extended care. Your breathing is stable, infection is resolving, and your heart rhythm is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve come a long way. Continue the IV antibiotics and steroids as prescribed. Watch for fever, breathing trouble, or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I get sick again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be brought back to the hospital. That’s what you wanted. But no intubation or CPR. Your MOLST form is clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’m ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will take you shortly. Take care, and follow up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—we checked your labs this morning. Sodium is 128, WBC is 16.6, but you’re not febrile. Likely due to hemoconcentration from diuresis. Keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no more changes to meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just continue as planned. The rehab team will check sodium and CBC in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your brother confirmed he understands your wishes. He’ll be your contact.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: He’s good about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final X-ray shows improvement in lung findings. No effusion. PICC line is still in place but will be removed after antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t like having it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll arrange for home health to remove it. You’re doing well. Just keep up the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge team is finalizing your meds. You’ll get nebs, steroids, and potassium daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I need my thyroid and blood pressure pills too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home meds are included except what’s replaced by IV treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared for transport. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll be in touch with the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in before you leave. Still feeling okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Stay safe and follow the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Transport is here. Have a safe trip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___ . I’m Dr. ___ . You’re in the hospital because your white blood cell count came back very high during a routine check at your clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: White blood cells? I feel fine. Why am I here again? I don’t remember being in the hospital recently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You were just discharged a few days ago after being treated for low oxygen and blood pressure, likely from food or saliva going into your lungs—what we call aspiration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I guess that sounds familiar. But I’m breathing okay now. No cough or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Your breathing is stable, and your oxygen level is 97% on two liters of oxygen. But your white blood count was 19,100, which is high, and it went up to 21,000 at the clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that infection? Do I need antibiotics again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked for infections—blood, urine, and stool—and all came back negative. No sign of C. diff or a urinary infection. So we don’t think it’s a new infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then why is it high?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely due to ongoing irritation in your lungs from small amounts of food or saliva getting in—what we call aspiration pneumonitis. It causes inflammation, not infection, so your body is reacting with more white cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not sick? But I’ve been eating like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. As long as you’re eating by mouth, there’s a risk of this happening. Your family and care team know this, and you’ve chosen to continue eating, accepting that risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to eat. It’s one of the things I still enjoy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We respect that. That’s why we’re not starting antibiotics—you just finished a course, and we don’t want to overuse them unless truly needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my sodium? I remember they said it was low last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 117, but we corrected for your high blood sugar, and it’s actually 123. That’s still low, but better than last admission. We’re keeping your fluids limited to 1200 mL a day to help it improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t like drinking much anyway. Is it getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s slowly improving. We’ll keep monitoring it. Your heart rate is a bit slow, so we held your metoprolol for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that for years. Atrial fibrillation, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, paroxysmal AFib. We’ll restart the metoprolol once your blood pressure is more stable. Your heart rhythm looks regular now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my breathing? The chest X-ray—did it get worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray shows some persistent changes in your lungs, but no new pneumonia. It’s mostly the same as before—diffuse interstitial opacities, likely from chronic lung issues and past aspiration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the PICC line? I remember they put one in last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the left PICC line is still there, but it’s not in the right spot—it ends in your axilla, not the central vein. So today, we’re placing a new one in your right arm to make sure we can give medications safely if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another line? Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use numbing medicine, so you’ll just feel some pressure. It’s a quick procedure, and the nurse will help you through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The new PICC line was placed successfully in your right arm. The X-ray confirms it’s in the right spot—upper right atrium. The old one on the left will stay for now but won’t be used.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I didn’t feel much. Is everything else okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your labs today show your white count went up slightly to 20,600, but still no signs of infection. Your sodium improved to 128, which is good progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not getting antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, because we don’t see evidence of infection. Your body is reacting to the ongoing irritation from aspiration, not a new bug. We don’t want to use antibiotics unless absolutely necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about my blood? I remember being low before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin was 7.0, which is low, but stable. No signs of bleeding. It’s likely chronic anemia from your medical history. We’re not transfusing—you’re not having symptoms like chest pain or severe fatigue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do get tired, but I always have.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’re managing your other conditions—COPD, heart disease, thyroid—with your regular meds. We added miconazole powder for the rash in your groin—it’s a fungal infection, common in warm, moist areas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that itch. I’m glad you noticed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve done well overnight. Your vitals are stable—pulse 62, blood pressure 128/70, oxygen 95% on two liters. We’re planning to discharge you today to the extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already? I feel about the same as when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And that’s good. You’re not worse. Your labs are stable, no infection found, and your sodium improved. We don’t need to keep you longer just for a high white count if you’re clinically well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When should I come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop fever, cough, increased shortness of breath, or feel unwell—then come back. But not just for a high white count. We expect that may happen again because of the aspiration risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I keep eating the way I am?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You and your family have made it clear—you want to eat, even with the risks. We support that. Just keep using thickened liquids, pureed food, and the chin-tuck technique with help from your caregivers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my DNR status still stands?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, DNR/DNI is confirmed. But we will still treat any new medical issues—like infections or heart problems—if they arise and you want that care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to live as I am, with dignity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And that’s exactly what we’re supporting. The team will send your updated meds and instructions to your care facility. You’ll continue your breathing treatments, heart meds, and the miconazole for the rash as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate the honesty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get the discharge papers ready. A nurse will help you down to transport in about an hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my brother is my health care proxy. He knows everything, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we spoke with him yesterday. He understands your condition, the risks of aspiration, and your wishes. He’s listed as your contact.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I feel ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure everything is set. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. You're here because you were having trouble breathing at your nursing home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s hard to catch my breath. But I’ve felt like this before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. Your oxygen levels were low when EMS arrived—75%—and they improved to 88% with a mask. We’re keeping you on oxygen now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m always dizzy too. And cold. But no fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your labs show your sodium is low, which can cause dizziness. That’s been a long-standing issue for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I threw up something dark on the way here. Coffee ground, they said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s concerning for a stomach bleed. We gave you medicine to reduce stomach acid and checked your blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I going to need a transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin was stable at first, but we’re watching it. We may give you blood if it drops further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My stomach feels a little sore, but not bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep an eye on that. Your chest X-ray shows long-standing lung changes, likely from repeated aspiration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I aspirate. But I want to keep eating. It’s important to me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve reviewed your goals. You and your family have chosen comfort care, no feeding tube, and no resuscitation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I just want to be comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back with no growth, so there’s no sign of active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started them initially, but given your goals and no clear infection, we’ve stopped them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I don’t want to be on more meds than necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We agree. We’re focusing on comfort. Your breathing is still labored, and we’re not using the BiPAP machine since you didn’t tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It made me feel worse. I prefer the mask.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll stick with the face mask. Your white blood cell count is high, but that’s likely from chronic aspiration, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Same pattern. We’re not seeing new pneumonia, just ongoing inflammation from aspiration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my stomach? Any more bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No further episodes. We transfused one unit of blood yesterday, and your levels have stabilized.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to keep losing blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring closely. Your heart rhythm is still atrial fibrillation, but your rate is controlled with metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that for years. No blood thinners, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. Because of your history of bleeding and falls, you’re not on warfarin. You’re on aspirin for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing has worsened overnight. Your oxygen levels are dropping even with the mask.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s harder to talk now. Feels like I’m drowning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. Your lungs are filled with inflammation from repeated aspiration. It’s not getting better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve spoken with your brother, your healthcare proxy. Given your DNR status and comfort goals, we’re shifting fully to comfort care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. No machines. Just keep me comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue your nebulizers for comfort and stop any non-essential medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Stop the statin, the thyroid pill, the sleeping pill. I don’t need them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discontinue those. Your brother agrees. We’re focusing only on what keeps you comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is even more labored today. We’ve increased your oxygen, but your body is tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so tired. Just want to rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here with you. Your brother has been informed. We’re making you CMO—comfort measures only.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Tell my brother I love him.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I will. We’ll keep you as comfortable as possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing has slowed. You’re very peaceful now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Just rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re staying right here with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your brother is on his way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not alone.
